scenes.headline: How eight vLLM changes speed up Gemma 4 E2B
scenes.sub: Mostly one idea: do not compute rows nobody reads.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Pennywhistle! Gemma's team reported a big speedup for a small model in vLLM. Most of it comes from one idea, and I'll show you where.

scenes.text: Twenty of the thirty-five layers only read cached keys, so a prompt needs them for one row per request.
scenes.say: The idea: twenty layers only read another layer's cache, so during a prompt they need to run for just the one row that produces the next token.

steps.say: Every prompt row runs through the first fifteen layers. Those layers write the keys and values that everything later will read.
Then only the row that will be sampled is kept. The other rows stop here.
The twenty shared layers read the cache and run on that one row, then the head scores the next token.

scenes.label: of the layer weight work sits in the shared layers
scenes.note: counted from the checkpoint's tensor shapes
scenes.say: By tensor shapes, sixty-nine point nine percent of the layer weight work is in the shared layers. That is the work a prompt can skip.

left.title: Fewer launches
left.say: Fused kernels, simpler metadata and more work inside a captured graph all cut launches and memory round trips.

right.title: Better tiles
items: Sliding window starts at its edge
right.say: Attention tiles are tuned for the big head size, and sliding window decode starts at the window edge instead of the beginning.

scenes.text: Most of the gain is skipping rows the shared layers never needed, then removing overhead around it.
scenes.say: So most of the gain is skipping rows the shared layers never needed. The rest is removing overhead around that.
To recap: shared layers only read a cache, a prompt needs one row from them, and you should check parity on your own prompts.
